title: Violin Concerto No. 1 in G minor
hook: A prelude, a great slow song and a dance; the concerto that eclipsed everything else its composer wrote.

painting.title: Iphigenia
painting.pairingNote: Painted by a German Romantic a few years before the concerto, a woman gazing out to sea in silent longing; the same long, singing line as Bruch’s Adagio.

facts: Bruch finished the first version in 1866, while he was music director in Koblenz. It was first played on 24 April 1866 by the violinist Otto von Königslow, with Bruch conducting.
He then revised it thoroughly with the help of the great violinist Joseph Joachim. Joachim gave the first performance of the final version in Bremen on 7 January 1868.
The first movement is not a full sonata movement but a *Vorspiel*, a prelude, that leads straight into the slow movement. The Adagio is the heart of the concerto.

Bruch sold the score outright to his publisher, Simrock, for a small lump sum, so its huge success earned him little. He grew tired of violinists who played only this concerto and ignored his others. Left poor by the First World War, he sent the manuscript to America to be sold; he died in October 1920 without receiving any money for it.
bigPicture.inOneLine: a dramatic prelude with free solo passages (I), a long, glowing song (II), a fiery dance in double stops (III).

movements.heading: Vorspiel: Allegro moderato
movements.summary: A prelude, not a conventional first movement. The woodwinds ask a quiet question and the violin answers alone, freely, like a singer improvising. Then come a passionate main theme and a gentler second one, and at the end the opening question and answer return. Instead of finishing, the movement flows straight into the Adagio.

mainIdeas.name: The question
mainIdeas.description: a soft drum roll, then a short, solemn phrase in the woodwinds and horns.

mainIdeas.name: The answer
mainIdeas.description: the solo violin alone, rising freely from its lowest note, like a short [[cadenza|cadenza]].

mainIdeas.name: The main theme
mainIdeas.description: a passionate, surging melody for the violin, in G minor.

stops.hear: A very soft drum roll; woodwinds and horns play a short, solemn phrase
The violin alone answers, climbing from its lowest note to a long high note
The question and the answer again, the answer now wider
The violin launches a passionate, surging melody; the orchestra drives it on
stops.happening: The main theme, in G minor

stops.hear: Calmer: the violin sings a slower, tender melody
The violin climbs and races; the orchestra bursts in loudly
The main theme briefly returns, then the tension rises again
The woodwind question and the violin’s answer return, now more brilliant

stops.label: Last minute
stops.hear: The orchestra builds a powerful climax and fades; one low note in the violins holds and leads on

notice: The movement ends where it began, with the woodwind question and the violin’s free answer. Compare the two versions.
Listen to the last seconds: the movement never really stops. A single held note carries you into the Adagio.

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: Mutter recorded the concerto with Karajan and the Berliner Philharmoniker in September 1980, when she was seventeen. On the Spotify album the Bruch is tracks 4–6, after Mendelssohn’s concerto. Because the first movement runs straight into the Adagio, the break between tracks 4 and 5 falls in continuous music.

movements.heading: Adagio
movements.summary: The heart of the concerto: a slow, warm song in E-flat major. The violin sings almost without a break, while the orchestra keeps moving underneath, so the music always seems to flow. Two melodies alternate and grow, rising to a passionate climax before the movement fades in peace.

mainIdeas.name: The first melody
mainIdeas.description: a long, expressive line that rises slowly and keeps unfolding.

mainIdeas.name: The second melody
mainIdeas.description: broader and darker, a contrast to the first.

stops.hear: Out of the held note, the violin begins a slow, warm melody
stops.happening: The first melody, in E-flat major

stops.hear: The melody climbs and swells; the woodwinds answer
A broader, darker melody on the violin
The music grows more urgent; the orchestra swells beneath the violin
The first melody returns, richer, with the orchestra fuller around it
The second melody returns at full strength; the violin soars over the whole orchestra

stops.label: Last 90 seconds
stops.hear: Calm; long, soft, high notes on the violin; the movement fades away

notice: Listen under the violin. The orchestra hardly ever stops moving, even when the melody is at its slowest.

movements.heading: Finale: Allegro energico
movements.summary: A fiery dance. After a quiet, tense build-up in the orchestra, the violin bursts in with a theme played in [[double-stop|double stop]]s, two notes at once. A broad, singing second melody keeps cutting in, but the dance wins and the concerto ends in a rush.

mainIdeas.name: The dance
mainIdeas.description: a vigorous, leaping theme in G major, played in double stops.

stops.hear: Quiet, tense chords in the violas, then the violins; the dance is hinted at and grows
The solo violin bursts in loudly with a leaping dance, playing two notes at a time
stops.happening: The main theme, in double stops

stops.hear: The whole orchestra takes up the dance
The orchestra plays a broad, warm melody; then the violin takes it
The dance returns and is worked through new keys
The leaping theme in double stops again
The broad melody once more, now in G major

stops.label: Last 70 seconds
stops.hear: Faster and faster, climbing higher; two short, grand chords

notice: Listen to the violin’s first entry. You hear two notes at once, which is what makes the theme sound so full and rough.

threads.title: A prelude and a song
threads.body: The first movement exists to lead into the Adagio; the two belong together and run without a break.

threads.title: The violin as singer
threads.body: In his day Bruch was known above all for choral music, and the solo part is written like a long vocal line.

threads.title: Free and strict
threads.body: The free, improvised-sounding solo passages of the first movement set off the regular rhythm of the dance at the end.
